subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A sole proprietorship is a form of business which is-

options.A: owned by a single individual but controlled and operated by a board of managers appointed by him
options.B: owned and controlled by two or more individuals who share the profits and losses in an agreed ratio
options.C: owned by a single individual whose liability for the debts of the business is limited to his capital
options.D: owned, controlled and operated by a single individual who is the sole beneficiary of all profits or loss

answer_html:
Answer: (D) owned, controlled and operated by a single individual who is the sole beneficiary of all profits or loss.

A sole proprietorship can be explained as a form of business or an organisation that is owned, controlled and operated by a single individual who is the sole beneficiary of all profits or loss and is responsible for all risks. It is a popular form of business, especially suitable for small business at least for its initial years of operation.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In a sole proprietorship business, the sole owner has-

options.A: liability limited to the assets of the business
options.B: no personal liability for the debts of the business
options.C: unlimited liability
options.D: liability limited to his capital

answer_html:
Answer: (C) unlimited liability.

Among the features of a sole proprietorship are that the business is formed by the owner himself, that the legal formalities relating to formation and closure are the minimum, that the sole owner has unlimited liability, that he alone bears all the risks related to the business, and that he controls all the business activities as all the rights and responsibilities lie with him.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: As regards the proprietor and his business-

options.A: both the law and accounting treat them as one and the same entity in every respect
options.B: both the law and accounting treat them as two separate and independent entities
options.C: the law makes no distinction between them, but in accounting they are considered as two separate entities
options.D: the law makes a distinction between them, but in accounting they are considered as one and the same entity

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the law makes no distinction between them, but in accounting they are considered as two separate entities.

The law does not make any distinction between the sole proprietor and his business. However, while accounting, the owner and the business are considered as two separate entities, which is an application of the business entity concept.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The components of the financial statements of a sole proprietorship include-

options.A: the Manufacturing Account, the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet
options.B: the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account, the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and the Balance Sheet
options.C: the Manufacturing Account, the Trading Account, the Balance Sheet and the Cash Flow Statement
options.D: the Trial Balance, the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the Manufacturing Account, the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet.

While finalising the accounts, a sole proprietorship prepares financial statements to determine its financial results and its financial state of affairs. The components accordingly include the Manufacturing Account, which is prepared only in the case of manufacturing entities, the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A sole proprietorship firm does not prepare a Profit and Loss Appropriation Account because-

options.A: the entire profit is attributable to the sole owner
options.B: the profit of such a firm is never distributed at all
options.C: the appropriation of profit is shown in the Trading Account instead
options.D: the law does not permit such a firm to appropriate its profit

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the entire profit is attributable to the sole owner.

Sole proprietorship firms do not require any Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, as the entire profit is attributable to the sole owner. In a partnership or a company, by contrast, the profit has to be divided among more than one claimant and an appropriation account becomes necessary.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A Trading Account is prepared to determine-

options.A: the gross operating results, that is the gross profit or gross loss
options.B: the net operating results, that is the net profit or net loss
options.C: the financial position of the business on a specific date
options.D: the cost of the goods manufactured during the period

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the gross operating results, that is the gross profit or gross loss.

The Trading Account is prepared by a non-corporate trading business entity to determine the gross operating results, that is the gross profit or gross loss. Its principle involves matching the cost of goods sold of an accounting period against the corresponding sales, and it considers only the direct costs and the direct income for the determination of gross profit or gross loss.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Trading Account is a nominal account and is closed by the transfer of the gross profit or gross loss to the-

options.A: Manufacturing Account of the period
options.B: Profit and Loss Account
options.C: Capital Account of the proprietor
options.D: Balance Sheet of the business

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Profit and Loss Account.

The Trading Account is a nominal account and is closed by transfer of the gross profit or gross loss to the Profit and Loss Account. It is the Profit and Loss Account which is in turn closed by transfer of the net profit or net loss to the capital account of the proprietor.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Profit and Loss Account is closed by the transfer of the net profit or net loss to the-

options.A: Manufacturing Account of the period
options.B: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
options.C: Capital Account of the proprietor
options.D: Trading Account of the period

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Capital Account of the proprietor.

The Profit and Loss Account determines the net profit or net loss of the organisation for a particular accounting period by charging the indirect expenses and losses against the gross profit and other indirect incomes, and it is closed by transfer of the net profit or net loss to the capital account of the proprietor, the profits belonging to the owner of the business.
topic_text: Closing of the Profit and Loss Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Balance Sheet is the financial statement prepared to show-

options.A: the financial results of the organisation for a period
options.B: the cost of the goods manufactured during the period
options.C: the movement of cash into and out of the organisation
options.D: the financial position of the organisation on a specific date

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the financial position of the organisation on a specific date.

The Balance Sheet is the financial statement prepared to show the financial position of the organisation on a specific date. It is prepared after drafting the income statements, that is the Trading Account and the Profit and Loss Account, and it reflects the assets and liabilities of the concern at a particular point of time.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A Manufacturing Account is prepared to determine-

options.A: the value of the closing stock of finished goods
options.B: the cost of goods manufactured
options.C: the cost of goods sold during the year
options.D: the gross profit earned during the year

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the cost of goods manufactured.

The Manufacturing Account is prepared only by a manufacturing organisation and is prepared to determine the cost of goods manufactured, the difference being transferred to the Trading Account. Its debit side includes opening work-in-progress, raw materials consumed, direct labour, direct expenses and factory overhead costs, and its credit side includes the closing work-in-progress only.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In the Balance Sheet, fixed assets are always shown as-

options.A: original cost less depreciation
options.B: original cost without any deduction
options.C: market value on the date of the balance sheet
options.D: original cost less the amount realisable on sale

answer_html:
Answer: (A) original cost less depreciation.

Fixed assets represent the facilities or resources owned by the business for a longer period, the basic purpose of which is not to buy and sell them but to use them for future earnings. They are subject to wear and tear, which is called depreciation, and in the balance sheet fixed assets are always shown as original cost less depreciation.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The financial results and the financial state of affairs of a sole proprietorship are determined respectively by-

options.A: the Balance Sheet and the Income Statement
options.B: the Trial Balance and the Income Statement
options.C: the Income Statement and the Trial Balance
options.D: the Income Statement and the Balance Sheet

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the Income Statement and the Balance Sheet.

While finalising the accounts a sole proprietorship entity prepares financial statements to determine its financial results by the Income Statement and its financial state of affairs by the Balance Sheet. The Income Statement comprises the Trading Account and the Profit and Loss Account.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A bank overdraft represents the amount-

options.A: held by the business at its bankers on the date of the balance sheet after all cheques have been cleared
options.B: utilised over and above the balance in the account as approved by the bank in the form of a short-term loan
options.C: deposited with the bank over and above the minimum balance which the bank requires to be maintained
options.D: lent by the bank against a charge on the fixed assets of the business for a period exceeding one year

answer_html:
Answer: (B) utilised over and above the balance in the account as approved by the bank in the form of a short-term loan.

A bank overdraft is listed among the short-term or current liabilities and represents the amount utilised over and above the balance in the account as approved by the bank in the form of a short-term loan. Long-term liabilities, by contrast, are normally obtained against some security such as a charge on the fixed assets and are called secured loans.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The debit side of the Manufacturing Account includes-

options.A: opening work-in-progress, raw materials consumed, direct labour and all the office and selling expenses
options.B: closing work-in-progress, raw materials consumed, direct labour, direct expenses and factory overheads
options.C: opening work-in-progress, raw materials consumed, direct labour, direct expenses and factory overhead costs
options.D: opening stock of finished goods, purchases, direct labour, direct expenses and factory overhead costs

answer_html:
Answer: (C) opening work-in-progress, raw materials consumed, direct labour, direct expenses and factory overhead costs.

The debit side of the Manufacturing Account includes the opening work-in-progress, being the balance of goods yet to be finished, raw materials consumed, direct labour, direct expenses and factory overhead costs. The credit side includes the closing work-in-progress only, and the difference, being the cost of goods manufactured, is transferred to the Trading Account.
topic_text: Debit side of the Manufacturing Account

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Direct expenses debited to the Trading Account mean all those expenses incurred-

options.A: in the administration of the office of the business, such as office salaries, printing, stationery and audit fees
options.B: in raising the finance required by the business, such as interest on loans, bank charges and discount allowed
options.C: from the time of purchase to making the goods in suitable condition, such as freight inward, octroi and wages
options.D: after the goods have been made ready for sale, such as freight outward, advertising and salesmen's commission

answer_html:
Answer: (C) from the time of purchase to making the goods in suitable condition, such as freight inward, octroi and wages.

Direct expenses mean all those expenses which are incurred from the time of purchases to making the goods in suitable condition, and these expenses include freight inward, octroi and wages. The expenses described in Option (D) are selling and distribution expenses and those in Option (A) administrative expenses, both of which are charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The deductions which may be made from purchases in the Trading Account include-

options.A: purchase returns, goods lost by fire and the provision made for doubtful debts
options.B: purchase returns, goods withdrawn by the proprietor and goods distributed as free samples
options.C: sales returns, goods withdrawn by the proprietor and goods distributed as free samples
options.D: purchase returns, carriage inwards and the closing stock of finished goods on hand

answer_html:
Answer: (B) purchase returns, goods withdrawn by the proprietor and goods distributed as free samples.

Purchases include cash as well as credit purchases, and the deductions which can be made from purchases are such items as purchase return, goods withdrawn by the proprietor and goods distributed as free samples. Sales returns, by contrast, are deducted from sales on the credit side of the Trading Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: According to the convention of conservatism, the closing stock is valued at-

options.A: cost or net realisable value, whichever is higher
options.B: cost in every case, whatever the net realisable value may be
options.C: net realisable value in every case, whatever the cost may be
options.D: cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower

answer_html:
Answer: (D) cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.

In the case of a trading business there will be closing stocks of finished goods only, and according to the convention of conservatism stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower. Where the market price of the unsold stock is higher than its cost, therefore, the stock is still carried at cost.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A gross profit arises where the credit side of the Trading Account is greater than the debit side, and a gross loss-

options.A: where the debit side is greater than the credit side
options.B: where the credit side is greater than the debit side
options.C: only where the closing stock is less than the opening stock
options.D: only where the sales for the year are less than the purchases

answer_html:
Answer: (A) where the debit side is greater than the credit side.

If the credit side of the Trading Account is greater than the debit side, a gross profit will arise, and when the debit side of the Trading Account is greater than the credit side, a gross loss will appear. In each case the balancing figure is transferred to the Profit and Loss Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Abnormal losses such as stock destroyed by fire and goods lost in transit are charged against-

options.A: the Trading Account
options.B: the Manufacturing Account
options.C: the Capital Account of the proprietor
options.D: the Profit and Loss Account

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the Profit and Loss Account.

All abnormal losses are charged against the Profit and Loss Account, and they include stock destroyed by fire and goods lost in transit. The Profit and Loss Account is also debited with the cost of sales and with all the other expenses which are not directly related to the main business activity, such as administrative, selling and distribution expenses.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: On the credit side of the Profit and Loss Account, commission received and discount received are classified as revenue incomes, while interest received and dividend received are classified as-

options.A: other incomes, being purely incidental and not arising from the main activity
options.B: revenue incomes likewise, since they too arise in the ordinary course of business
options.C: abnormal gains, being amounts which the business does not expect to earn again
options.D: capital receipts, which are carried directly to the capital account of the proprietor

answer_html:
Answer: (A) other incomes, being purely incidental and not arising from the main activity.

Revenue incomes are those which arise in the ordinary course of business and include commission received and discount received. Other incomes are those which the business generates otherwise than from its main activity and are purely incidental, and they include items such as interest received and dividend received.
topic_text: Credit side of the Profit and Loss Account

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The arrangement of the items in the Balance Sheet in a specific order is known as marshalling, of which the approaches are-

options.A: the liquidity order, the profitability order and the solvency order
options.B: the rigidity or permanence order, the liquidity order and the mixed order
options.C: the rigidity or permanence order, the liquidity order and the horizontal order
options.D: the horizontal order, the vertical order and the mixed order

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the rigidity or permanence order, the liquidity order and the mixed order.

The various items should appear in the Balance Sheet in a specific order which is known as marshalling, and there are three approaches in this respect, namely the rigidity or permanence order, the liquidity order and the mixed order. The horizontal and vertical arrangements referred to in Options (C) and (D) are formats of presentation, not orders of marshalling.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Under the liquidity order of marshalling-

options.A: assets are arranged in order of liquidity while liabilities are arranged in order of rigidity
options.B: assets are arranged in order of rigidity while liabilities are arranged in order of liquidity
options.C: fixed assets come after the current assets and long-term liabilities come after the current liabilities
options.D: fixed assets come before the current assets and long-term liabilities come before the current liabilities

answer_html:
Answer: (C) fixed assets come after the current assets and long-term liabilities come after the current liabilities.

Under the liquidity order, non-current or fixed assets come after the current assets and non-current or long-term liabilities come after the current liabilities. Option (D) describes the rigidity or permanence order, and Option (A) the mixed order, in which asset side items are arranged in order of liquidity while liability side items are arranged in order of rigidity.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Current liabilities are liabilities expected to be settled within the same accounting period or operating cycle, and include-

options.A: loans from banks and financial institutions obtained against a charge on the fixed assets
options.B: the capital of the proprietor together with the net profit for the year added to it
options.C: sundry creditors, advances from customers, outstanding expenses, bills payable and bank overdrafts
options.D: sundry creditors, advances to suppliers, prepaid expenses, bills receivable and bank balances

answer_html:
Answer: (C) sundry creditors, advances from customers, outstanding expenses, bills payable and bank overdrafts.

Short term or current liabilities are those expected to be settled within the same accounting period or the same operating cycle, and the items listed are sundry creditors, advances from customers, outstanding expenses, bills payable and bank overdrafts. The items in Option (D) are current assets and those in Option (A) long-term liabilities.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Fixed assets are distinguished by the fact that-

options.A: the basic purpose of these resources is not to buy and sell them but to use them for future earnings
options.B: they are held primarily for the purpose of being traded in the normal operating cycle of the business
options.C: they are expected to be realised or consumed within one year from the date of the balance sheet
options.D: they are funds invested outside the business on a temporary basis pending their being required

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the basic purpose of these resources is not to buy and sell them but to use them for future earnings.

Fixed or non-current assets represent the facilities or resources owned by the business for a longer period of time, and the basic purpose of these resources is not to buy and sell them but to use them for future earnings, the benefit from their use being spread over a very long period. Option (B) describes current assets and Option (D) investments.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Current investments are distinguished from non-current investments in that current investments-

options.A: are made in the fixed assets of another business and are subject to depreciation year by year
options.B: are by their nature readily realisable and are intended to be held for not more than one year from the date of investment
options.C: are restricted beyond the current period as to their sale or disposal and are intended to be held permanently
options.D: are made out of the surplus funds of the business and are never shown in the balance sheet at all

answer_html:
Answer: (B) are by their nature readily realisable and are intended to be held for not more than one year from the date of investment.

Investments are funds invested outside the business on a temporary basis and are classified into current investments and non-current investments. Non-current investments are those which are restricted beyond the current period as to sale or disposal, whereas current investments are by their nature readily realisable and are intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which the investment is made.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In the Balance Sheet, sundry debtors are shown-

options.A: after adding the provision for bad debts, so as to state the total claim outstanding against customers
options.B: after reducing the bad debts or the provision for bad debts, the net figure being carried to the balance sheet
options.C: at their gross figure, the bad debts and the provision for bad debts being shown on the liabilities side
options.D: at their gross figure, no deduction being permitted until the debts are actually proved irrecoverable

answer_html:
Answer: (B) after reducing the bad debts or the provision for bad debts, the net figure being carried to the balance sheet.

Debtors represent customer balances which are not paid, and the bad debts or a provision for bad debts is reduced from debtors and the net figure is shown in the balance sheet. The same treatment is applied to any provision for discount on debtors, which is deducted from the resulting figure.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Carriage inward and freight outward are respectively shown in-

options.A: the Trading Account on the debit side and the Profit and Loss Account on the debit side
options.B: the Profit and Loss Account on the debit side and the Trading Account on the debit side
options.C: the Trading Account on the debit side and the Trading Account on the credit side
options.D: the Profit and Loss Account on the debit side and the Profit and Loss Account on the credit side

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the Trading Account on the debit side and the Profit and Loss Account on the debit side.

Carriage inward is a direct expense incurred in bringing the goods to a saleable condition and is debited to the Trading Account, whereas freight outward is a selling and distribution expense incurred after the goods are ready for sale and is debited to the Profit and Loss Account. Wages and power and fuel go to the Trading Account, while salaries to office staff, insurance, audit fees and bad debts go to the Profit and Loss Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Return outwards and return inwards are respectively shown in the Trading Account-

options.A: on the credit side as a deduction from sales and on the debit side as a deduction from purchases
options.B: on the debit side as an addition to purchases and on the credit side as an addition to sales
options.C: on the credit side as an addition to sales and on the debit side as an addition to purchases
options.D: on the debit side as a deduction from purchases and on the credit side as a deduction from sales

answer_html:
Answer: (D) on the debit side as a deduction from purchases and on the credit side as a deduction from sales.

Purchase returns or return outwards appear in the Trading Account on the debit side, being deducted from purchases, while return inwards or sales returns appear on the credit side, being deducted from sales. Each is thus netted against the item to which it relates rather than shown as a separate item on the opposite side.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where a trial balance shows the same head in both columns, the item appearing in the debit column in the case of returns, discounts and commission means respectively-

options.A: purchase return, discount received and commission received
options.B: sales return, discount received and commission allowed
options.C: purchase return, discount allowed and commission received
options.D: sales return, discount allowed and commission allowed

answer_html:
Answer: (D) sales return, discount allowed and commission allowed.

Returns in the debit column mean sales return while those in the credit column mean purchase returns. Discounts in the debit column mean discount allowed, which is an expense, and those in the credit column mean discount received, which is an income, and commission is treated in the same way, the debit column meaning commission allowed and the credit column commission received.
topic_text: Returns, discounts and commission in the trial balance

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where a trial balance contains both 'Wages and Salaries' and 'Salaries and Wages', the accepted interpretation is that-

options.A: both items are taken to the Trading Account, since wages appear in the description of each of them
options.B: both items are taken to the Profit and Loss Account, since salaries appear in the description of each
options.C: where the first reference is to wages it is taken to the Trading Account and where the first reference is to salaries it is taken to the Profit and Loss Account
options.D: where the first reference is to wages it is taken to the Profit and Loss Account and where the first reference is to salaries it is taken to the Trading Account

answer_html:
Answer: (C) where the first reference is to wages it is taken to the Trading Account and where the first reference is to salaries it is taken to the Profit and Loss Account.

Where the first reference is made to wages, the item is assumed to be directly for goods and is taken to the Trading Account, and if the first reference is to salaries the item is assumed to be related to the office and is taken to the Profit and Loss Account. Thus Wages and Salaries goes to the Trading Account and Salaries and Wages to the Profit and Loss Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In the case of a sole proprietorship, income tax is-

options.A: viewed as a personal obligation and recorded by debiting the Capital Account rather than the Profit and Loss Account
options.B: treated as an ordinary business expense and recorded by debiting the Profit and Loss Account of the firm
options.C: treated as an ordinary business expense and shown as a current liability without any debit to any account
options.D: not recorded in the books of the business at all, being a matter entirely outside its accounting records

answer_html:
Answer: (A) viewed as a personal obligation and recorded by debiting the Capital Account rather than the Profit and Loss Account.

In the case of companies, income tax payable is treated as an ordinary business expense. However, for sole proprietorships income tax is viewed as a personal obligation and is recorded by debiting the capital account rather than the profit and loss account, the entry being Capital A/c Dr., to Income Tax A/c. This is because the amount of the tax depends on the total income of the proprietor besides the profit of the firm.
topic_text: Income tax of a sole proprietor
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In the case of a partnership business, where the firm pays income tax on behalf of the partners, such payment of personal income tax is treated as-

options.A: a charge against the capital reserve
options.B: drawings
options.C: an expense of the firm
options.D: an asset of the firm

answer_html:
Answer: (B) drawings.

In the case of a partnership business, the firm's own tax liability is debited to the profit and loss account of the firm, but the partners' tax liability is not to be borne by the firm. Therefore, if the firm pays income tax on behalf of the partners, such payment of personal income tax should be treated as drawings.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
case_facts_html:
A manufacturing concern presents the following figures for the year ending 30th June 2023. The opening stocks were raw material ₹1,20,000, work-in-progress ₹24,000 and finished goods ₹86,400, and the closing stocks were raw material ₹80,000, work-in-progress ₹16,000 and finished goods ₹64,000.

The transactions during the year were purchase of materials ₹4,00,000, wages ₹2,50,000, stores consumed ₹30,000, indirect wages ₹72,000, factory rent ₹24,000 and depreciation on plant and machinery ₹40,000.

Sales for the year were ₹11,20,000 and purchases of finished goods were ₹10,000. A Manufacturing Account and a Trading Account are to be prepared.
question_html: Refer to the third case scenario. The cost of goods manufactured which is transferred to the Trading Account is-
answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹8,64,000.

The Manufacturing Account is debited with the opening stocks of raw material and work-in-progress of ₹1,20,000 and ₹24,000, purchases of materials ₹4,00,000, wages ₹2,50,000, stores consumed ₹30,000, factory rent ₹24,000, depreciation ₹40,000 and indirect wages ₹72,000, that is ₹9,60,000. It is credited with the closing stocks of raw material and work-in-progress of ₹80,000 and ₹16,000, that is ₹96,000, so the cost of goods manufactured is ₹8,64,000.

case_facts_html:
A manufacturing concern presents the following figures for the year ending 30th June 2023. The opening stocks were raw material ₹1,20,000, work-in-progress ₹24,000 and finished goods ₹86,400, and the closing stocks were raw material ₹80,000, work-in-progress ₹16,000 and finished goods ₹64,000.

The transactions during the year were purchase of materials ₹4,00,000, wages ₹2,50,000, stores consumed ₹30,000, indirect wages ₹72,000, factory rent ₹24,000 and depreciation on plant and machinery ₹40,000.

Sales for the year were ₹11,20,000 and purchases of finished goods were ₹10,000. A Manufacturing Account and a Trading Account are to be prepared.
question_html: Refer to the third case scenario. The stocks which enter the Manufacturing Account are-

options.A: raw material, work-in-progress and finished goods, all three appearing in the Manufacturing Account
options.B: work-in-progress and finished goods only, the raw material appearing in the Trading Account
options.C: raw material and finished goods only, the work-in-progress appearing in the Trading Account
options.D: raw material and work-in-progress only, the finished goods appearing in the Trading Account

answer_html:
Answer: (D) raw material and work-in-progress only, the finished goods appearing in the Trading Account.

The Manufacturing Account carries the opening and closing stocks of raw material and work-in-progress, together amounting to ₹1,44,000 on the debit side and ₹96,000 on the credit side. The opening and closing stocks of finished goods of ₹86,400 and ₹64,000 belong to the Trading Account, which also carries the sales and the purchases of finished goods.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Opening stock of raw materials was ₹12,000, purchases of raw materials ₹2,50,000 and closing stock of raw materials ₹14,000. Opening work-in-progress was ₹6,000 and closing work-in-progress ₹7,000, and the other manufacturing costs were factory wages ₹1,75,000, factory rent ₹10,000, salary of the factory manager ₹80,000 and depreciation on machinery ₹10,000. The raw materials consumed and the cost of goods manufactured are respectively-
answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹2,48,000 and ₹5,22,000.

The raw materials consumed are ₹12,000 plus ₹2,50,000 less ₹14,000, that is ₹2,48,000. The debit side of the Manufacturing Account then totals ₹6,000 plus ₹2,48,000 plus ₹1,75,000 plus ₹10,000 plus ₹80,000 plus ₹10,000, that is ₹5,29,000, from which the closing work-in-progress of ₹7,000 is deducted, leaving a cost of goods manufactured of ₹5,22,000.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A trader's opening stock was ₹10,000, purchases ₹1,60,000, return outward ₹10,000, carriage inwards ₹10,000, wages ₹30,000 with ₹4,000 outstanding, freight ₹8,000 of which ₹1,000 was prepaid, royalty on production ₹6,000 and gas and fuel ₹2,000. Sales were ₹3,00,000 with return inward ₹16,000, closing stock at cost was ₹20,000, stock of ₹10,000 was destroyed by fire, goods of ₹6,000 purchased and still in transit were unrecorded, and goods of ₹3,000 were taken by the proprietor. The gross profit is-
answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹98,000.

Purchases become ₹1,60,000 less return outward ₹10,000 and goods taken by the proprietor ₹3,000 plus goods in transit ₹6,000, that is ₹1,53,000, wages become ₹34,000 and freight ₹7,000. The debit side therefore totals ₹2,22,000. The credit side is sales of ₹2,84,000 plus closing stock of ₹20,000, the stock destroyed of ₹10,000 and the goods in transit of ₹6,000, that is ₹3,20,000, giving a gross profit of ₹98,000. The goods in transit are added to both purchases and closing stock and are therefore neutral in effect.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Sundry debtors stood at ₹40,000, the existing provision for bad debts at ₹4,000 and bad debts already written off at ₹2,000. Further bad debts of ₹2,000 are to be written off and a provision of 5% is to be made on sundry debtors. The new provision and the net amount credited to the Profit and Loss Account in respect of the provision are respectively-
answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹1,900 and ₹2,100.

The new provision is computed on the debtors after deducting the further bad debts, that is 5% of ₹40,000 less ₹2,000, or 5% of ₹38,000, which gives ₹1,900. The old provision of ₹4,000 is credited to the Profit and Loss Account and the new provision of ₹1,900 deducted from it, leaving ₹2,100 credited. Computing the provision on the full ₹40,000 would give the ₹2,000 in Option (A).

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A trader's Trading Account totalled ₹8,65,000 on each side and yielded a gross profit of ₹2,89,250. The Profit and Loss Account was debited with salaries ₹30,000, rent, rates and taxes ₹12,000, printing and stationery ₹2,250, depreciation ₹3,020, repairs ₹6,000, export duty ₹9,000, discount allowed ₹12,505, bad debts ₹9,000, advertisement ₹2,500 and general expenses ₹4,000. The net profit is-
answer_html:
Answer: (C) ₹1,98,975.

The expenses charged to the Profit and Loss Account total ₹90,275, and deducting these from the gross profit of ₹2,89,250 leaves a net profit of ₹1,98,975. Export duty of ₹9,000 is a selling expense charged to the Profit and Loss Account and not to the Trading Account, which is where coal and coke, gas and water, factory lighting, carriage and wages belong; omitting it would give the figure in Option (D).
